2	
3	## Register

11	## Users
12	
13	People who meet a lot of others over a life -- through work, events, travel, friends of friends -- and who want to stay connected instead of letting those relationships quietly lapse.
14	The defining moment of use is recall: you half-remember someone (a name fragment, where you met, one detail) and you want to find your way back to them so you can reach out.
15	There is one audience, the person keeping their own memory layer. Nothing here is shared, social, or multi-user; every person and note is private to the owner.
16	Success looks like a user opening Euno, finding the person they were reaching for, and leaving to actually reconnect.
17	
18	## Product Purpose
19	
20	Euno is a personal memory layer over the people of your life. Social media and contacts help with the first connect, not with maintaining a relationship over time; Euno is that maintenance layer.
21	Its one job is to help you find back the people you have met, from whatever fragment of memory you bring, so you can keep the connection alive.
22	The core loop is small on purpose: search or add a person, add a link and whatever context you want to remember, save, and return to search. The value is the quiet handoff at the end -- the right person, given back.
23	
24	## Positioning
25	
26	Bring a fragment of memory; Euno gives you back the person. It is the one place built to refind the people you have met, not to collect, rank, or broadcast them.
27	
28	## Brand Personality
29	
30	Calm, focused, content-first. The voice is warm, plain, and unhurried -- it talks like a person, never like a product demanding attention.
31	The feeling to leave a user with is quiet relief: the small, grounding moment of being handed back someone you had half-forgotten. Nothing urgent, nothing loud, nothing that performs.
32	
33	## Anti-references
34	
35	Not a social network: no feeds, likes, follower counts, activity streams, or engagement mechanics. Euno is private and quiet, not something you perform in.
36	Not a CRM or sales tool: no pipelines, deal stages, lead scoring, or dashboards of metrics. These people are relationships, not leads to work.
37	
38	## Design Principles
39	
40	Hand back the person, not a dashboard. Every screen earns its place only if it helps return a person from a fragment of memory. The search box and the person are the heroes; everything else stays quiet.
41	
42	No scoring, no judgment. Euno never ranks closeness, grades how well you know someone, or nags you to reconnect before you lose them. It holds memory; it does not keep score. Recency (when added, when last touched) exists only to keep the screen useful, never as a health signal.
43	
44	The tool disappears into the task. One primary action per screen. Content leads, chrome recedes. Familiar, trustworthy affordances over invented ones, so the interface never asks the user to stop and figure it out.
45	
46	Quiet by default. Restraint in color, motion, and copy. Depth and softness (gentle shadows, large radii, spring-like transitions) carry the feel, not decoration or noise. Motion conveys state, never demands attention.
47	
48	Private and personal. This is one person's memory layer. Nothing is shared or observed; the design should always feel like a private space, not a network.
49	
50	## Accessibility & Inclusion
51	
52	Target WCAG 2.2 AA. Body text holds at least 4.5:1 contrast, interactive controls show a visible focus state, and touch or click targets stay large and forgiving.
53	Respect the system: follow light and dark preference, and honor prefers-reduced-motion with a calm non-animated fallback for every transition.

88	# Design System: Euno
89	
90	## 1. Overview
91	
92	**Creative North Star: "The Quiet Room"**
93	
94	Euno is a calm, private space where a person is gently handed back to you. The whole visual
95	system exists to get out of the way: the search box and the person are the heroes, and every
96	other pixel steps back so they can lead. Depth is soft, color is rare, and motion only ever
97	confirms that something happened. Nothing here performs, competes for attention, or asks the
98	user to stop and figure it out.
99	
100	The palette is drawn from Apple's platform conventions on purpose. Familiarity is the feature:
101	a person opening Euno should feel like they already know how it works. The system stack, the
102	16px rounded surfaces, the single blue reserved for the one action worth taking -- these are
103	trustworthy defaults, not brand flair. The design earns quiet by leaning on what people already
104	recognize, then removing everything else.
105	
106	The Quiet Room explicitly rejects two neighbors. It is not a social network: no feeds, follower
107	counts, activity streams, or engagement mechanics. It is not a CRM: no pipelines, stages, scores,
108	or dashboards of metrics. These are relationships, not leads, and Euno never grades how well you
109	know someone. The interface should always feel like a private room, never a stage and never a
110	sales floor.
111	
112	**Key Characteristics:**
113	- Content-first: one primary action per screen, chrome recedes.
114	- Familiar by design: the system font stack and platform-native blue.
115	- Flat surfaces, soft lift: hairline borders at rest, gentle shadow only when something floats.
116	- Rare accent: a single blue, spent only on the primary action, focus, and selection.
117	- Calm motion: 140-280ms confirmations on a strong ease-out; the only element that ever
118	  travels between screens is the tapped name.
119	- Light and dark as equals, following the system preference.
120	
121	## 2. Colors
122	
123	A near-monochrome system where a single blue is the only saturated voice, and everything else is
124	a quiet ramp of neutral ink on soft surfaces.
125	
126	### Primary
127	- **Signal Blue** (#0071e3 light / #0a84ff dark): The only accent in the system, named for its
128	  job -- it signals the one action worth taking. Used on primary buttons, the focus glow ring,
129	  and the current selection. Never used for decoration, dividers, or backgrounds.
130	- **Signal Blue, text grade** (#0069d5 light / #0a84ff dark): The tinted-text variant for ghost
131	  buttons and inline links. The light value sits one step deeper than the fill so 17px text
132	  holds 4.8:1 on the canvas. Filled buttons keep #0071e3 in both modes, so white labels hold
133	  4.7:1 everywhere.
134	
135	### State
136	- **Quiet Red** (#d70015 light / #ff453a dark): Error text only -- a failed sign-in, a failed
137	  save. Both values hold 4.9:1 or better on their surfaces. Never a fill, never decorative.
138	
139	### Neutral
140	- **Ink** (#1d1d1f light / #f5f5f7 dark): Primary text. The person's name, the words the user
141	  typed, everything meant to be read.
142	- **Muted** (#6e6e73 light / #98989d dark): Secondary text only -- field labels, the sign-in
143	  tagline, quiet helper copy. Never body text.
144	- **Surface** (#ffffff light / #1c1c1e dark): The material that inputs, result rows, and cards
145	  are cut from. It sits one step above the canvas.
146	- **Canvas** (#f5f5f7 light / #000000 dark): The body background the surfaces rest on.
147	- **Hairline** (#00000014 light / #ffffff1a dark): The 1px border that defines a surface without
148	  drawing attention. An 8% (light) / 10% (dark) wash, never a hard line.
149	
150	### Named Rules
151	**The One Blue Rule.** Signal Blue is the only saturated color in the product outside the error
152	state's Quiet Red. If a screen shows blue in two unrelated places, one of them is wrong. Its
153	rarity is what makes the primary action unmistakable.
154	
155	**The Muted-Is-Not-Body Rule.** Muted gray (#6e6e73) is for labels and helper text only. Body
156	text is always Ink. Muted gray running as body copy is the fastest way to make a calm interface
157	read as washed-out and hard to read.
158	
159	## 3. Typography
160	
161	**Display Font:** System stack (-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif)
162	**Body Font:** Same system stack
163	
164	**Character:** One family, tuned by size and weight rather than by pairing. On Apple devices this
165	resolves to SF Pro, which is exactly the point -- the type should feel native and unremarked, so
166	the words carry the meaning and the letterforms never announce themselves.
167	
168	### Hierarchy
169	- **Display** (600, 28px, 1.1 line-height, -0.02em tracking): The person's name on the detail
170	  screen and the Euno wordmark on sign-in. The largest type in the product; there is no hero
171	  display scale above it because Euno never shouts.
172	- **Title** (600, 20px, 1.2, -0.02em): The Euno wordmark in the app header. Quiet brand presence,
173	  not a banner.
174	- **Body** (400, 17px, 1.5): Everything the user reads or types -- inputs, result rows, button
175	  labels, context. The workhorse size. Prose in the context field stays comfortable at 65-75ch.
176	- **Label** (400, 13px, muted): Field labels ("Link", "Context") and the sign-in tagline. Small,
177	  quiet, always in Muted gray.
178	
179	### Named Rules
180	**The Size-And-Weight Rule.** Hierarchy comes from size and weight, never from boxes, rules, or
181	color. If a heading needs a border or a background tint to read as important, the size and weight
182	are wrong.
183	
184	## 4. Elevation
185	
186	Flat by default, soft on lift. Surfaces rest flat, defined only by a 1px hairline border. Depth
187	appears in exactly two situations: when something genuinely floats above the page, and when a
188	control responds to focus. There is no ambient drop-shadow on ordinary cards and rows; stacking
189	them with shadows would read as heavier and busier than The Quiet Room allows.
190	
191	### Shadow Vocabulary
192	- **Floating panel** (`box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0,0,0,0.12)`): For a surface that is truly
193	  lifted off the page -- the sign-in card, and any future modal or sheet. Large, soft, and diffuse,
194	  never a tight dark drop shadow.
195	- **Focus glow** (`box-shadow: 0 0 0 4px color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent) 15%, transparent)`):
196	  A soft Signal Blue ring on the focused input, paired with an accent border. This is feedback,
197	  not decoration.
198	
199	### Named Rules
200	**The Flat-At-Rest Rule.** A surface at rest carries a hairline border and no shadow. Shadow is a
201	response to state (a panel that floats, a control that has focus), never a default coat of paint.
202	If it looks like a 2014 app, the shadow is too dark and the blur is too tight.
203	
204	## 5. Components
205	
206	### Buttons
207	- **Shape:** Full pill (980px radius). The one shape that reads as "tap me."
208	- **Primary:** Signal Blue background, white text, 500 weight, 17px, 12-20px padding. One per
209	  screen -- Save, Add, Sign in. This is where the product's only accent is spent.
210	- **Pressed:** A quiet 0.97 scale on :active (140ms, strong ease-out). Hover only deepens the
211	  fill slightly, and only on real pointers; the press is an acknowledgement, not a bounce.
212	- **Secondary / Ghost:** For Back, Sign out, and the sign-in mode toggle. Transparent
213	  background, Signal Blue text grade, pill-shaped hit target with a soft accent tint on hover
214	  and the same 0.97 press. Reads as an action the way platform text buttons do, without ever
215	  competing with the one filled pill.
216	
217	### Inputs / Fields
218	- **Style:** Surface background, 1px hairline border, 16px radius, 14-16px padding, 17px text.
219	  Large and forgiving to tap.
220	- **Focus:** Border shifts to Signal Blue and a soft 4px blue glow ring appears (150ms). The only
221	  moment an input carries color.
222	- **Error / Disabled:** Errors render as a 13px Quiet Red line near the control (sign-in, save),
223	  announced politely to assistive tech. Disabled controls drop to 55% opacity and refuse the
224	  press scale.
225	- **Search anatomy:** A muted magnifier sits inside the field, a circular clear button appears
226	  once there is text, and the input carries 44px side padding so type never collides with
227	  either.
228	
229	### Result Rows
230	- **Style:** A full-width tappable button styled as a Surface row -- hairline border, 16px radius,
231	  17px Ink text, left-aligned. The list of people the search returns.
232	- **Pressed:** A barely-there scale to 0.985 on :active (140ms), so the tap registers physically
233	  without motion drawing the eye. Hover is a 4% ink tint, gated to real pointers.
234	
235	### Cards / Containers
236	- **Corner Style:** 24px radius on the sign-in card (larger and softer than the 16px inputs it
237	  holds); 16px on inline surfaces.
238	- **Background:** Surface, on the Canvas body.
239	- **Shadow Strategy:** Floating panel shadow only when the card floats (sign-in). Inline surfaces
240	  stay flat per the Flat-At-Rest Rule.
241	- **Border:** 1px hairline.
242	- **Internal Padding:** Generous -- 32px 28px on the sign-in card. Let the content breathe.
243	
244	### Header
245	- **Material:** Sticky and translucent -- 78% canvas over a 20px blur with 180% saturation, so
246	  content scrolls under it like platform chrome. A hairline appears on its bottom edge only
247	  once content has actually scrolled beneath it. Reduced transparency gets a solid header.
248	- **Slots:** The wordmark on the search screen, the chevron Back ghost on the person screen,
249	  Sign out as a ghost on the right.
250	
251	### The Name Morph (signature)
252	The tapped name is the only element that travels between screens: the search row's text glides
253	into the detail title (280ms, strong ease-in-out) while the rest of the screen quietly
254	crossfades (180ms out, 220ms in). It is the product thesis rendered as motion -- you bring a
255	fragment, Euno hands you back the person. Browsers without the View Transitions API get a
256	260ms rise-and-fade instead; reduced motion gets an instant swap.
257	
258	### Layout
259	- **Frame:** A single centered column, max-width 640px, 24px page padding with safe-area
260	  insets. Euno is a phone-shaped reading width even on desktop; the person is meant to be
261	  read, not spread across a dashboard.
262	- **Responsive:** The column simply narrows on small screens. There are no sidebars, panels, or
263	  breakpoint-driven grids to collapse -- structure this simple does not need them.
264	
265	## 6. Do's and Don'ts
266	
267	### Do:
268	- **Do** spend Signal Blue only on the primary action, focus, and selection. One blue per screen.
269	- **Do** keep one primary action per screen; let the search box and the person lead.
270	- **Do** use Ink for anything meant to be read, and reserve Muted (#6e6e73) for labels and helper
271	  text only.
272	- **Do** keep surfaces flat with a hairline border at rest; add shadow only when something floats
273	  or takes focus.
274	- **Do** hold body text and placeholders at 4.5:1 contrast or better (WCAG 2.2 AA), and give every
275	  control a visible focus state.
276	- **Do** keep motion between 140ms (presses) and 280ms (the name morph) on the strong ease-out
277	  curve (cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)), and honor prefers-reduced-motion with an instant,
278	  non-animated fallback.
279	
280	### Don't:
281	- **Don't** build anything that reads as a social network -- no feeds, likes, follower counts,
282	  activity streams, or engagement mechanics. Euno is a private room, not a stage.
283	- **Don't** build anything that reads as a CRM or sales tool -- no pipelines, deal stages, lead
284	  scoring, or dashboards of metrics. These are relationships, not leads.
285	- **Don't** show a health score, closeness ranking, streak, or "reconnect before you lose them"
286	  nudge. Euno holds memory; it never grades a relationship.
287	- **Don't** run Muted gray as body text on a tinted surface; it reads as washed-out and fails
288	  contrast. Body is Ink.
289	- **Don't** introduce a second accent hue, a gradient, or gradient text. The system is one blue
290	  on neutrals.
291	- **Don't** add ambient drop shadows to ordinary cards and rows, or use a tight dark 2014-style
292	  shadow anywhere.
293

content.text:
I read PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md end to end. So this isn't me guessing - here's what Euno actually is, and then what I think it really means underneath.

## What it says it is

Euno is a private memory layer over the people you've met. Not the first handshake - social media and your phone's contacts already do that - but the part after, the slow erosion where relationships quietly lapse because nobody is holding the thread. The one job: you show up with a fragment (half a name, "we met at that thing in Lisbon," one weird detail you remember about them) and Euno hands the person back to you so you can go reconnect.

The whole thing is built as a refusal. Not a social network (no feeds, no likes, no follower counts). Not a CRM (no pipelines, no lead scores, no "reconnect before you lose them" nudges). Even the signature animation - the tapped name gliding from the search row into the detail title - is the thesis rendered as motion: you bring a fragment, it gives you back the person.

## What I think it actually means

Three things sit underneath the spec, and they're the real idea.

**1. It's fighting a specific kind of loss - not forgetting a fact, but losing a person.** Most tools optimize the moment of connection. Euno is the only one pointed at the long tail, where the cost isn't "I lost their email," it's "there was someone who mattered and I let them dissolve." That's a quietly emotional problem dressed as a utility. The product is a hedge against your own memory decay over a whole life.

**2. The restraint IS the product, not the packaging.** "No scoring, no judgment" isn't a design nicety - it's the entire moral stance. The second you rank closeness or show a streak, these people become metrics and the tool becomes a CRM that makes you feel guilty. Euno's bet is that the reason people don't keep a system like this is that every existing system turns relationships into work and judgment. So it removes the judgment. It holds memory; it refuses to keep score. That's a genuinely opinionated, almost counter-cultural stance in a world of engagement mechanics.

**3. The feeling it's selling is relief, not productivity.** Read the brand line again: "quiet relief - the small, grounding moment of being handed back someone you had half-forgotten." Most software wants to capture your attention. Euno wants to give you back the person and then get out of the way so you *leave the app*. Success is measured by the user exiting to go text a real human. That's rare, and it's the most honest thing about it.

## The one-sentence version

Euno is a private place to refind the people your life keeps scattering - built on the belief that the enemy isn't bad contact management, it's the slow forgetting, and that the cure is memory without judgment.

---

If I'm being a real thinking partner and not just a mirror, here's the tension worth watching: the same restraint that makes Euno beautiful is also its hardest growth problem. A tool with no feed, no notifications, no social loop, and whose success is you *leaving* has almost no built-in reason to pull you back. The whole product lives or dies on that recall moment being so good it becomes a reflex - "who was that person" becomes "open Euno" the way "what's that word" became "open a dictionary." The import ideas in your memory (LinkedIn, Apple Contacts) matter for exactly this reason: an empty memory layer can't hand anyone back, so getting the people *in* without it feeling like data entry is the quiet make-or-break.

Want me to pressure-test any of this - the positioning, the retention risk, or whether the "no judgment" stance holds up once someone has 2,000 people in there?

content.text:
Everything's actually wired in - not dormant. Love Alarm lives inside the search screen, shared notes inside the person detail. So here's Euno read purely from the code, docs closed.

## What the code literally builds

**The spine is a private people table.** Each row is one person you've met, owned by your Clerk identity, holding a name, a link, and freeform context. Nothing about that row is visible to anyone else by default.

**But recall is engineered hard.** That table carries *three* ways back to a person: a normalized-name text search, and a 1536-dimension vector embedding index for semantic search. You don't need the name - you can find someone by the shape of what you remember about them. The single most invested-in capability in the backend is "given a fragment, return the person."

**Intake is designed to cost almost nothing.** The `captures` flow: you upload a screenshot of someone's profile, a paid AI model extracts platform, name, handle, headline, bio, and it becomes a person. Meeting someone and remembering them is reduced to one screenshot.

**Each person is rendered as their own patch of the universe.** `sky.ts` deterministically mints a unique star field - nebulae, giants, constellation edges, a shooting star - from a person's identity. Same person, same sky, forever. The signed-out landing is literally "Euno" rendered as its own sky. The metaphor isn't decoration; it's the core object.

**And then the part the code builds that a pure "private vault" would never need:**
- `profiles` - a public in-the-moment Euno handle
- `connections` - a mutual link both people must accept, each bound to their own private person row
- `sharedNotes` - a note two connected people co-write, wired live into the person screen
- `loveAlarm` - room-code proximity presence: join a code, heartbeat every minute, 2-minute TTL, and `nearby` shows who else is in the room *right now*. It sits inside the search screen.
- `eunoContactUserId` - "Euno Meet," an idempotent in-person exchange so two Euno users meeting face-to-face each get a private row for the other

## The meaning, from code alone

Euno is a personal universe of the people you cross paths with - captured the instant you meet them, and navigable back from any fragment of memory forever.

It spans the whole arc of a relationship, not just one end of it:
- **The moment you meet** - Love Alarm sees who's physically near you right now, Euno Meet exchanges you with another user in one tap, a screenshot turns a stranger's profile into a remembered person.
- **The long tail** - private context plus semantic recall so nobody dissolves out of your memory.
- **The optional shared thread** - for people who are also on Euno, a mutual connection and a note you both keep.

Each person held as their own constellation you can return to. That's the thesis the code commits to: turn the scatter of everyone you've ever met into a night sky you can always find your way across.

## The honest divergence worth knowing

The docs (which you told me to ignore, and I did) insist Euno is *"nothing shared, social, or multi-user... every person and note is private"* and explicitly *not* about the first connect. **The code contradicts that.** It ships public handles, mutual connections, shared notes, in-person exchange, and real-time proximity presence - a whole social, in-the-moment, first-connect layer, all live and wired into the UI.

So one of two things is true: either PRODUCT.md/DESIGN.md are stale and describe an earlier, purer idea the code has since outgrown - or the code is running ahead of the stated product and someone needs to decide whether Euno is "the quiet solo memory room" or "the network for the people you meet in person." Right now the code has quietly become the second thing while the docs still swear it's the first.

Want me to dig into whether that social layer is actually reachable end-to-end by a normal user (can two people really connect today?), or is it half-built scaffolding wearing a finished coat?
